commit 7ce3e77dfbca80bfa2ab3c73a84e0454570d7158
Author: Colin McDonnell <3084745+colinhacks@users.noreply.github.com>
Date:   Mon Aug 24 22:51:20 2026 -0700

    fix(v4): run a wrapper's inner schema on its own payload (#6462)
    
    A pipe hands its `out` schema the caller's issues array, so an unrecognized key can survive to an enclosing intersection that may yet reconcile it. Two wrappers on the far side of that pipe read someone else's issue as their own inner failing, substituted for it, and cleared the array.
    
    For `.catch()` that lost the strict violation, and where an intersection was the reason the key was forwarded at all, it substituted the fallback into one side of the merge and threw `Unmergable intersection` out of `safeParse`. `.optional()` over a defaulted inner had the same hole. Neither wrapper had any business substituting: `z.any()` cannot fail and a default cannot fail.
    
    Both fired because they shared a payload with their inner schema and so could not tell whose issues they were looking at. The inner now gets a payload of its own, as it did in v3 and as the compiled path already did. Everything that existed to undo the inner's damage to the shared payload goes with it — the pre-run value capture, the defensive copy of the issues array, and the truncation and abort resets in both wrappers. `issues.length = 0` no longer appears anywhere in `core/`.
    
    One flag is carried across by hand. The memoizer marks a payload whose value is a node still being parsed, and that mark describes the value, which still propagates. Without it an enclosing readonly froze a half-built object — silently dropping a key under the JIT, and throwing `TypeError` out of `parse` for records, tuples, arrays and jitless objects — and a check on the back-edge ran against the in-progress node.
    
    Bundle is 2 B smaller raw and 5 B smaller gzipped on a classic fixture, unchanged on `zod/mini`. Retained bytes per schema are identical, and failure-path allocation drops about 24 B per parse with no measurable change on the success path.
    
    Refs #6192

commit 7cfc012238ca88ff4aa87a22e8fa08f5efb5b63d
Author: Colin McDonnell <3084745+colinhacks@users.noreply.github.com>
Date:   Mon Aug 24 19:54:14 2026 -0700

    fix(v4): keep a wrapper's stored value only on the side it belongs to
    
    `.default()` and `.catch()` store an output-side value; `.prefault()` stores an
    input-side one, since it is fed through the schema rather than short-circuited.
    The projections rewrote the inner type and left those values behind, so each
    landed on a side it could not belong to:
    
        const C = z.codec(z.string(), z.number(), { decode: Number, encode: String });
    
        z.input(C.default(7)).parse(undefined);      // 7, out of a ZodType<string, string>
        z.input(C.catch(9)).parse(123);              // 9, likewise
        z.output(C.prefault("5")).parse(undefined);  // threw invalid_type
    
    z.input now sheds a default and a catch, and z.output sheds a prefault. A
    default becomes optional rather than vanishing, because `.default()` widens the
    declared input type with `undefined` and z.input has to keep accepting it;
    `.catch()` leaves that type alone, so its inner schema stands on its own.
    
    All of it only when the projection actually rewrote the inner type. A wrapper
    over a pipe-free schema keeps both its value and its identity, so z.input of an
    object full of plain defaults is still that same object. visit already knew
    whether it had replaced anything below a node and did not pass it on, so it
    does now; deepPartial ignores the argument.

commit 3063993a3317ac8af7a244691b837fce3e53aa96
Author: Chris Cook <chris.zirkel@gmail.com>
Date:   Thu Aug 13 07:48:45 2026 +0200

    perf(v4): cut per-schema memory ~90% by moving methods to the prototype (#6318)
    
    Schema instances carried their methods as own properties, which put them past the point where V8 stops using inline slots for property storage. Moving those methods to the prototype — where they materialize per instance on first read — cuts a schema's retained size by roughly 90% and makes construction several times faster.
    
    - `z.string()` 7709 → 816 bytes retained; a 10-key object 83928 → 12171; `zod/mini` `z.string()` 2528 → 593
    - a 500-schema API catalogue holds 62.7 MB instead of 198.0 MB
    - construction is 45–83% faster; parse throughput is unchanged
    - bundle grows by a fixed ~150–200 B gzipped (+1% classic, +5% mini), the one axis that regresses
    
    Detachability is preserved — the getters bind on first access and cache, so `const { parse } = schema` and `arr.map(schema.parse)` still work — and descriptor attributes, enumerability and function-identity aliases were diffed against `main` across every schema type to keep the observable surface intact.
    
    Original work and the core insight by @zirkelc.

@@ -35,12 +35,45 @@ The project uses pnpm workspaces. Key commands:
 - Ask before generating new files

+- Any change to `packages/zod/src` must be weighed on **all three axes: runtime performance, memory consumption, and bundle size** — see "The three axes" below. A change that improves one and is only checked on that one is not finished.
 - ALWAYS use the `gh` CLI to fetch GitHub information (issues, PRs, etc.) instead of relying on web search or assumptions
 - Keep JSDoc as minimal as possible. A self-explanatory type or symbol name needs no doc comment. When a comment is genuinely required, write one short sentence describing behavior — not history, rationale, or examples. Don't add interface-level JSDoc that just restates the interface name.
 - When you've modified a PR (or opened/closed/commented on one), include the PR URL liberally in summary messages — at minimum once at the end of any reply that touched it
 - When creating a PR, do not include a separate test plan section in the body. Link to any relevant issues under discussion, and use the same copywriting guidelines from "Commenting on issues and PRs": concise maintainer voice, prose over templates, and validation details only when they are material to the reader.
 - NEVER bump the version in `packages/zod/package.json` (or any package's `package.json`). A version bump is the only thing that triggers a release; everything else (including direct pushes to `main`) is recoverable until that happens. If a version bump is genuinely needed, ask first.
 
+## The three axes
+
+Zod is judged on **runtime performance**, **memory consumption**, and **bundle size** at once, and they trade against each other constantly. Optimizing one in isolation is how regressions land: a change that buys bundle bytes can cost construction speed, and one that saves memory can cost both. Any non-trivial change to `packages/zod/src` — and any change to `core/` at all, since every build ships it — needs a number on all three before it is done. Report them together, including the ones that got worse.
+
+`zod/mini` deserves its own line on the bundle axis: it is sold on size, so a fixed cost lands very differently there (~200 B is 6% of the smallest mini bundle and 1% of classic's).
+
+| axis    | how to measure                                                                                                                                    |
+| ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
+| runtime | `packages/bench/*.ts` via `pnpm bench <name>`, plus construction cost — parse and construction move independently                                 |
+| memory  | `packages/bench/memory/schema-footprint.ts` and `realworld.ts` (retained bytes per schema; run under `--expose-gc`)                               |
+| bundle  | bundle a `packages/treeshake` fixture with esbuild `--minify` under `--conditions=@zod/source` and gzip it, for both a classic and a mini fixture |
+
+### Benchmarking traps
+
+These produced hours of wrong conclusions; check them before believing a number.
+
+- **Check `uptime` first.** A loaded machine invents effects of ±16%. Numbers taken above a load average of ~8 are worthless.
+- **Interleave the two revisions.** Running all of A then all of B puts any drift entirely on whichever ran second. Alternating round-by-round took per-side spread from 2.5x to 4%.
+- **Loading two zod revisions into one process makes call sites polymorphic.** It is fine for comparing construction, unreliable for tight leaf parses.
+- **Allocating benchmarks can't be timed by a fixed-duration loop.** `z.array().parse()` allocates per call, so a time-boxed harness samples whatever the collector is doing — it gave +8.2% and −17.3% on consecutive identical runs. Use a fixed iteration count with `gc()` between samples and take the minimum.
+- **Make sure the work isn't optimized away.** If a micro-benchmark reports ~1e9 ops/sec, V8 eliminated the loop; consume the result.
+
+### Property placement, specifically
+
+Most of the memory in a schema is its own-property count, not its closures. V8 sizes an instance's backing store in steps and `$constructor` assigns nothing itself, so instances get no in-object slots: **≤12 own properties cost 128 bytes, 13–20 cost 848, ≥21 cost 1616** (`packages/bench/memory/prop-slack.ts` measures this). Members therefore live on the prototype and materialize per instance on first read.
+
+If you touch that machinery, three things bite:
+
+- **Moving a property between definition sites changes its descriptor**, and writability/enumerability/configurability are part of the public contract. `packages/bench/memory/` has a surface-diff approach for this: dump every descriptor, alias and assign/delete semantic on both revisions and diff them. It caught four real regressions that tests did not.
+- **Redefining an accessor demotes the object to dictionary mode**, which cost 2x on `z.object().parse` once. Run `packages/bench/memory/dict-mode.ts` after any change here — every instance must report `fast`.
+- **A bound function pays a call-time trampoline.** Fine for cold builder methods, measurably not fine on the parse path.
+
 ## Cutting a release
 
 Only do this when the user explicitly asks. Pushing a version bump to `main` triggers `.github/workflows/release.yml`, which publishes to npm + JSR and creates a `v<version>` GitHub release. There is no undo.

    fix(locales): backfill the mac and Sizable.map gaps, and pin dictionary parity (#6427)
    
    Three keys had drifted the same way credit_card did in #6424: a feature
    shipped en and never backfilled the rest. Sizable.map arrived with #5316
    (ZodMap sizing) and was missing from 43 of 60 locales; mac arrived with #5440
    (MAC validation) and was missing from 49; Hebrew alone also lacked uuidv4,
    uuidv6 and template_literal.
    
    Only some of that is user-visible, and the distinction is worth recording.
    A missing FormatDictionary key renders the raw key name, which reads fine for
    emoji/nanoid/cuid/cuid2 because en maps those to themselves -- they are left
    alone deliberately. mac rendered lowercase "mac" instead of "MAC address". A
    missing Sizable.map is worse than either: it drops the unit and the verb, so
    German said "erwartet, dass map >=2 ist" where en says "expected map to have
    >=2 entries".
    
    Most strings are derived from the file's own vocabulary rather than composed:
    mac from that locale's ipv4 with the protocol token swapped, Sizable.map from
    that locale's set entry.
    
    Approximations, all deliberate:
    
    - Sizable.map copies set's unit everywhere. en distinguishes "entries" from
      "items"; most locales will not want to. be/hy/ru mirror set's plural forms
      rather than the precise word for entries.
    - fi needed its own genitive rather than a copy, since its subject field names
      the container: "kuvauksen". Finnish Map terminology is unsettled and this is
      the weakest string here; "sanakirjan" is the alternative.
    - az takes English "MAC address" to match its own untranslated ipv4/ipv6/cidrv4.
    - ur spells the acronym letter by letter, matching how that file already
      handles json_string, jwt and cuid.
    
    da, nn, no and sv all have ipv4 meaning "range" rather than "address"
    ("IPv4-omraade", "IPv4-intervall"), which their own email entries contradict.
    Deriving mac from those would have said "MAC range", so all four are written
    out instead. The ipv4 strings themselves are left as they are -- that is a
    separate change.
    
    The parity test is the point of the commit. It reads the key lists out of
    en.ts at test time instead of hardcoding them, so adding a format to en
    extends it automatically, and it exempts keys en maps to themselves by
    probing whether en falls through. A hand-maintained list would miss the next
    drift the way the last four were missed.
    
    Co-authored-by: Colin McDonnell <colin@colinhacks.com>

    Tighten cuid() regex and deprecate CUID v1 (#5880)
    
    - Change cuid regex from `/^[cC][^\s-]{8,}$/` to `/^[cC][0-9a-z]{6,}$/`
      in v4. Restricts the body to base36 (the actual CUID v1 charset) and
      aligns the length floor with Eric Elliott's documented guidance
      ("starts with c, contains at least 7 chars", paralleldrive/cuid#88).
      Brings the regex stylistically in line with the other ID validators
      (ulid, xid, ksuid, nanoid, cuid2), all of which use allowlist
      character classes.
    
      The change is backwards-compatible for any real CUID v1 output
      (always lowercase base36) and additionally accepts shorter cuid-shaped
      values that the prior `{8,}` floor incorrectly rejected. It rejects
      the punctuation-shaped false positives reported in #3621 and similar.
    
    - Mark CUID v1 surfaces `@deprecated` (function, chain method, schema
      class, internals, regex export) pointing at z.cuid2(). Per the
      upstream repo, "Deprecated collision-resistant id spec. Insecure
      because it leaks timestamps. Use cuid2 instead."
    
    - Add regression tests asserting that previously-accepted non-base36
      payloads are now rejected. Update one template-literal test that was
      relying on the old {8,} floor.
    
    Zod 3 is in maintenance mode and is intentionally left untouched.
